title: SLA-tradeoff-speedrun-deck-sketch
content:
Purpose: rapid 8-slide / 6-minute tech+ops run for platform sellers and SEs to use in discovery or 1:1s with platform engineering leads.

Context / why this exists:
- Customers are balancing latency SLOs vs token cost vs predictability of throughput. Sellers need a single, repeatable mini-deck and a set of one-liners + battlecards to move conversations from vague "we need low latency" to concrete engineering tradeoffs (batching, quantization, routing, dedicated vs hosted).
- This is intentionally terse — for rapid rehearsal and A/B with SEs. Treat as living notes; drop into a slide template later.

Audience (persona focus):
- Primary: Platform engineering / infra lead at mid-market / enterprise (manages internal ML infra, cares about capacity planning, SLAs, and upgrade risk).
- Secondary: Product teams (owner of latency SLAs for a feature), Integration architects.

Core narrative (6 min):
1) Problem framing (30s): "LLM features are great until they become the critical path — high variability in latency and cost kills adoption."
2) What we believe (30s): "You want predictable tail-latency and bounded cost; we give knobs to move cost <-> tail behavior with measurable outcomes."
3) Two-minute demo/visual (90s): show three routing outcomes: Hosted low-latency variant, Dedicated reserved GPU pool, and Cheap-quantized fallback. Include numeric examples (p50/p95/p99, cost per 1k tokens).
4) Canaries + fallbacks (60s): how automatic fallback policies and model variants keep the app live during overload. Quick checklist for handoff to SRE.
5) Simple math (30s): show sample monthly bill delta for 100M tokens with batching + KV cache vs naive per-request serving.
6) Ask + next step (30s): "If you care about p99 <= 200ms and 30% cost saving target, let’s run a 2-week pilot: pilot scope + what we need from them."

Slide-by-slide bullets (sketch):
- Slide 1 (title): SLA tradeoff speedrun — 6-min ops sprint
- Slide 2 (problem): short bullets + one chart: feature latency vs adoption curve (sketch)
- Slide 3 (knobs): batching, quantization, routing policies, dedicated pools, caching — one-line effect each
- Slide 4 (three-path example): table with p50/p95/p99 + cost per 1k tokens for Host/Dedicated/QuantizedFallback
- Slide 5 (canary & fallback flow): mini flowchart, quick Ops checklist for rollouts
- Slide 6 (rehearsal script): SE speaker notes + one-liners for common pushback
- Slide 7 (pilot plan): 2‑week tasks, success metrics, roles (seller, SE, customer infra contact)
- Slide 8 (appendix): data sources, links to evals, how we measure quality drift

Battlecard snippets (ready-to-say lines):
- Objection: "We can host models ourselves, why Redwood?"
  - Reply: "For predictable economics and built-in fallbacks — you can own model variants, but we provide the runtime orchestration, SLO routing, and cost tooling that lowers ops TCO. We tie the knobs to measurable per-token cost and p99s so your SREs can plan capacity instead of firefight."
- Objection: "Quantization reduces quality, we can’t risk it."
  - Reply: "We use tiered quantization: high-fidelity on canary traffic + automatic fallback to full-precision for sensitive prompts. We’ll validate with your eval prompts; if you want, we gate quantization on accuracy thresholds in the pilot."
- Objection: "What happens during a major traffic spike?"
  - Reply: "Routing policies escalate to dedicated pools, then to lower-cost variants with a degradable quality policy; we also expose immediate abort/slow-path controls to SREs. We provide a runbook and a post-mortem bundle for any incident."

SE rehearsal cheats (quick):
- 30s opener: "Most customers accept small latency increases if it guarantees availability and predictable cost — we help align on which tradeoffs matter to you."
- 45s demo cue: lead with p99 numbers + cost delta, avoid model internals unless asked
- 20s close: "Pilot looks like: 2 weeks, 3 success metrics (p99 target, cost delta, functional correctness on 10 eval prompts)."

Pilot template (2 weeks):
- Week 0 (prep): sync on metrics, get eval prompt set, grant read-only logs + sample traffic capture (we provide helper script).
- Week 1 (run): baseline measurements, enable batching + caching profiles, measure quality on eval set daily.
- Week 2 (stress + rollouts): run synthetic spike, enable canary fallback, review rollback criteria, finalize SLA handoff doc.

Quick technical appendix (one-liners for SEs):
- Batching: reduces per-token cost by X-40% depending on sequence distribution (call out: sensitive to variance in sequence length).
- KV cache: effective when user sessions repeat prefixes (e.g., chat apps) — can yield 60–80% token savings on repeated prompts.
- Quantization: recommend 4/8-bit profiles by workload; always validate on your eval set.
- Routing: prefer zone-local first; fallback to regional dedicated; last-resort quantized variant.

Open questions / TODOs (working list):
- Add p99/p999 sample numbers from our last Dedicated pilot (Mateo to paste).
- Create single-sheet pricing delta calculator for sellers (Priya owns prototype).
- Convert sketch to 8-slide deck in the new sales template and get 1st pass review from SE lead (Samira).
- Add a short customer-facing one-pager: "SLA tradeoff checklist" (deliverable for pilot kickoff).

Risks & mitigation notes (for SEs):
- Risk: customer treats cost-savings claims as guaranteed. Mitigation: call out assumptions (traffic shape, seq length distribution, cacheability).
- Risk: quantization perceived as feature regression. Mitigation: keep high-quality variant for critical prompts and use A/B on evaluation set.

Quick links for the deck (placeholders to replace before publish):
- Data sheet: CONFLUENCE-PLAT/SLA-TRADEOFFS-2024
- Pilot playbook: github.com/redwood-inference/pilot-playbooks/blob/main/sla-speedrun.md
- Incident runbook template: CONFLUENCE-PLAT/INCIDENT-RUNBOOK-TEMPLATE

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep examples concrete — sellers hate hypotheticals. Add two real pilot numbers (cost delta and p99 improvement).
- Run this by two SEs in practice session next Wed (book 30m).

End of sketch.
